title.narrative: ROAF/REG/Supporting Regional and National Efforts to Improve Land Governance and Resolve Land-Related Root Causes of Conflict in the Horn of Africa

description.narrative: This project has been designed to implement recommendations of the Scoping Study on Land and Conflict in the HoA , which identified the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) as the most appropriate strategic partner for interventions under Pillar Four of the Comprehensive Regional Prevention Strategy for the HoA to contribute to improvement of responsible land governance and enhance inclusive, equitable and sustainable development in the region. It will support IGAD, its Member States and other development actors in the region to implement regional level interventions to address land governance challenges and resolve land-related root causes of conflict. The Comprehensive Regional Prevention Strategy for the HoA, which was adopted in July 2019 provides the framework for delivering on the Special Envoy’s mandate of providing support to IGAD, other regional intergovernmental organizations, and countries of the region on peace and security, by enhancing sub-regional capacities for conflict prevention and mediation, and addressing cross-cutting issues. The Strategy specifies promoting sustainable natural resource development and climate resilience as one of the priority strategic concerns around which the Special Envoy will provide overall UN political leadership, leverage institutional knowledge, support resource mobilization efforts for regional interventions, and coordinate with other stakeholders. The Strategy commits the UN and its agencies to provide support to IGAD, its Member States and other development partners in the region to improve governance and management of natural resources as a means of creating better economic opportunities and reducing resource-based conflicts. To this end, the UN agencies working on Pillar Four of the Strategy will provide support to harmonization of policy, legal and institutional frameworks of regional governments and regional authorities for the sustainable use and management of the environment and natural resources and for managing the impacts of climate change. The Strategy was developed and adopted at a time when the HoA region was experiencing significant geopolitical shifts, including the rapprochement between Eritrea and Ethiopia and positive development in the diplomatic relations between Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia; the cooling-off of tensions between Djibouti and Eritrea; the lifting of the sanctions on Eritrea; the signing of the Revitalized Peace Agreement in South Sudan and the political transition in Sudan. These developments engendered hope and optimism about prospects for peace and stability in a region that had long been characterized by conflict, crises and instability. However, by the time of the scoping study in 2020, the optimism and hope that these shifts had ignited were waning, shaken by subsequent developments driven by both old and emerging challenges, including reversals in the South Sudan peace process, escalation of internal conflict in the Tigray Region of Ethiopia, and simmering border conflict between Kenya and Somalia. These developments emanated from and added to long standing challenges in the region that include unresolved border issues, tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), the ever-present threat of violent extremism, fragile electoral processes and shrinking of political space, competing external influences, soaring identity politics, a large and growing number of IDP/refugees, as well as flooding, drought, desert locusts and food insecurity, compounded by the existential threat posed by climate change or mega-trends such as cybercrime or widening inequalities. This volatile situation has been exacerbated over the past two years by the Covid-19 pandemic, which is having a multi-faceted impact on development, peace and security in the region. Conflicts have been a defining feature of the HoA for decades now, making it one of the most unstable regions in the world. Whether in the form of state-based, non-state or one-sided violence , conflicts have been endemic to the region, rendering livelihoods insecure, undermining development opportunities, exacerbating national and regional challenges to peace and prosperity, and exacting huge human and economic costs. Many of the conflicts in the region are underpinned by competition over access to land and natural resources. This is particularly so with regards to conflicts within and between communities. The importance of land as the main source of all material wealth, and the basis of livelihoods and economic development for the region, combined with the limited availability of productive land, rapid population growth and the adverse impacts of climate change, exacerbate this competition. The study underscored the important role of land governance in shaping the interaction between land and conflict, and affirmed that the frequency and severity of land related conflicts is often a result of the failure of land governance.
